thread.title: Apple's Moat Is Underestimated - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Nicholas Ward
title: Apple's Moat Is Underestimated - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Every morning I start my day by perusing various financial media outlets, reading relevant pieces to my holdings and current watch lists. Yesterday, an Apple ( AAPL ) related headline on Morningstar caught my eye. The piece was titled " Why We've Downgraded Apple's Moat Trend ".
As many of you probably know, Apple is my largest holding. Apple's ecosystem is a large part of my bullish thesis. Because of my overweight exposure to AAPL, I spend a lot of time monitoring the company as a part of my regular due diligence. Because of its negative headline, the Morningstar piece became a part of that due diligence process. Since the market has been relatively calm this morning, I decided to dedicate some time towards writing a response.
Admittedly, after reading the M* piece, I realized the headline's bark was worse than its bite. The analyst at Morningstar wasn't necessarily being bearish on AAPL. M*'s fair value estimate is lower than the current share price, at $175, but downgrading a moat seems scarier than a $10 move in share price. Instead, the author's thesis was essentially built around the fact that while AAPL's moat remains strong, it isn't widening. Assuming the M* analysts are focusing on hardware, I don't necessarily disagree with that.
However, AAPL is taking steps to make its ecosystem stickier. For instance, we recently saw a report that stated the company is considering bundling its services for users. I really like this idea. The Amazon Prime model is obviously working and while AAPL doesn't offer the eCommerce services that AMZN does, I think it could compete in music/video/social.
In today's digital day and age, consolidation is the name of the game. Consumers are flocking towards the simplest solutions. If AAPL can lock in iOS users across multiple devices into its own digital media channel, I think that bodes well for the stock long term.
As the M* article points out, Apple's genius comes from its ability to shape consumer sentiment by packaging "hardware, software, services, and third-party applications into sleek, intuitive, and appealing devices."
This is the equation that AAPL has used over the last decade or so to differentiate the iPhone from other smart phones. AAPL is famous for its profit margins in the mobile phone space where they're relatively hard to find for other companies. AAPL doesn't sell the most phones, but locks in the majority of the profits in this industry. I don't see any reason to believe that AAPL can't use its brand equity and proven advantages in the hardware space to succeed in the services/software space as well.
M* doesn't rate AAPL's moat as "wide", in part, because of the short-term product cycles in a highly competitive industry. If you're focusing purely on hardware, that's a valid point. Phones are only cool and new for a few months before the latest and greatest device is announced. Furthermore, I imagine it's only a period of time before phones become obsolete, as some other device takes their place filling the void in our day to day lives. However, I think this sort of hardware-centric mindset is missing the point.
It appears that Apple recognizes the fact that hardware sales are not going to be its bread and butter forever. They've already elongated their product cycles in response to waning demand for newer devices. As phone prices have risen, it's become more and more difficult for consumers to justify spending $1000 on a new device every year or two. I don't mind seeing the company prioritize margins over sales. Honestly, with other wearable devices on the market and coming down the pipelines of various technology firms, I wouldn't be surprised if we've seen "peak smartphone", at least in terms of short-term demand.
Do I think smart phones are going anywhere, anytime soon? No, and I don't know what comes next. Maybe it will be AR/VR enabled glasses/contact lenses. Maybe it will be brain implants. Honestly, I decided long ago that speculating about the future of technology is a waste of time, especially for someone like me that isn't in tune with the cutting-edge innovations coming out of Silicon Valley and the like.
It wasn't long ago that flip phones were innovative. Heck, I consider myself to be a young man, yet so much has changed in my lifespan thus far. It's amazing to consider the leaps and bounds technology has made in the last two decades. I'm sure that the new products and services created in the next couple of decades will be just as revolutionary.
But, with all of this being said, I do feel fairly comfortable saying this: whatever comes in the future, I'm sure AAPL will be in the center of it. The same thing goes for companies like Alphabet ( GOOGL ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Alibaba ( BABA ), etc. In my view, these big tech companies have amassed too much talent and have too many capital resources at hand to fail.
Maybe I'm being biased here (I'm long most of the notable "big tech" names worldwide). I've always believed that winning doesn't happen by accident and I feel comfortable betting on the big dogs. AAPL's massive cash hoard/cash flows enable it to participate in any major technological upheaval, so long as management doesn't become content/complacent with its current market position.
I don't think that Tim Cook and Co are content. I think that AAPL's growing services segment clearly shows this. I think this growing services segment is often overlooked by analysts and firms that come out with bearish stances on AAPL far too often. I think, to a certain extent, Morningstar in guilty of this. Sure, AAPL's moat in the hardware space might be narrow, but if you take a step back and look at this company from a broader perspective, it's difficult to find a better consumer-facing ecosystem in the technology space.
I will say that one could make the argument that there isn't a single technology company with a wide moat because of the innovative threats on all sides. I see the validity in that stance, though I also believe that's a slippery slope in terms of identifying moats in the market as a whole. The technology sector is certainly more volatile than many others, but there isn't a single sector out there where competition isn't fierce. That's the nature of free markets.
This isn't Morningstar's stance, anyway. I haven't taken the time to go through all of their economic moat data for the technology sector as a whole, but I did check a handful of well-known names and found that M* rates Alphabet, Facebook, Microsoft, and Amazon with wide moats.
Apple is being grouped with Netflix ( NFLX ) in terms of its narrow moat rating. Narrow is a step up from Spotify ( SPOT ), which is given a non-existent economic moat, so there's that. I suppose one might argue that this isn't a terrible place to be, being that NFLX has posted 100% plus returns year to date; however, I think it's unfair to say that AAPL and its wide variety of services across the iOS ecosystem is the same as Netflix, which only offers streaming services.
Apple's moat is as deep as its device count and as wide as the services they offer.
As hardware continues to become commoditized, its relative utility remains real. The practical utility of technology is where the long-term moat lies, in my opinion. What Apple has done with its iOS operating system is create a defensible business that can be replicated across platforms. As Apple adds devices to its stable, it draws more consumers into its web. I've heard arguments against the stickiness of Apple's ecosystem for as long as I've been following the markets. There always seems to be an issue with Apple's execution, innovation, capital management, etc… yet the sales, earnings, and share price continues to rise.
Not only has Apple taken steps to increase its active device count, offering a variety of hardware options for consumers with different user profiles, but the company has diversified the services that these devices are capable of as well. Apple moves slowly, but it moves deliberately. Sometimes, I think, you could even say that Apple moves sneakily because sometimes it seems as though the market doesn't realize that Apple is stronger than ever until it is stronger than ever.
M* refers to the iPhone as Apple's "crown jewel" and while I don't disagree, I think that could be changing in the near future. After years of being undervalued, I think this company sees the writing on the wall. With its services division, Apple is in a unique position to control its ecosystem, end to end. This is the moat that Apple has developed and with every quarter that posts double digit services growth, I think we're seeing Cook's plan come to fruition. And the best part about this ecosystem is that it's a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Once you're in, you're stuck. You've got no desire to leave because of the elegance of the systems they've created. Cash flows like Apple's don't happen by accident. It's as if the Hotel California was built in Cupertino.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, AMZN, MSFT, FB, BABA, GOOGL.
I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
